note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

unit.title: Plan to undertake a routine task

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A job card asks for 20 brackets 'the same as last month's order'. What should you still check before planning?
options: That the same welder is free to do the job
That last month's invoice has been paid
That the brackets can be painted a new colour
That the drawing has not been revised since then

questions.stem: The welding procedure for a job calls for E7018 electrodes, but the store only has E6013. What should you do?
options: Use E6013, since both are mild steel electrodes
Stop, and ask the supervisor before welding
Mix the two types to make the stock last
Weld with E6013 and say nothing about it

questions.stem: Why should the plan for a welded frame include a welding sequence?
options: So that the welder can finish before lunch
To balance the heat and keep distortion down
So that the frame uses fewer electrodes
To make the welds look the same colour

questions.stem: Put these steps for a small welded frame in the right order: 1 weld out, 2 cut and prepare, 3 tack and check square, 4 inspect and finish.
Why is a frame tacked and checked before it is fully welded?
options: Tacks make the frame lighter to carry
Full welds cannot be made without tacks
The inspector only checks tacked frames
Mistakes are easy to fix at that stage

questions.stem: What is a 'hold point' in a work plan?
options: A place in the shop where finished work is stored
The time of day when the team takes lunch
A stage where work waits for a signed check
The point on a frame where it is lifted

questions.stem: The drawing calls for 6 mm fillet welds, but the client's specification calls for 8 mm. Which is the best action?
options: Weld 8 mm, as a bigger weld is always safer
Weld 6 mm, as the drawing always comes first
Ask the engineer, and get the answer in writing
Weld 7 mm, as a fair point between the two sizes

questions.stem: A frame needs 4 pieces of 1,200 mm and 4 pieces of 800 mm, cut from 6 m lengths of square tube. Allowing 3 mm for each saw cut, how many 6 m lengths are needed?
A job has these steps: cutting 1.5 h, fit-up 2 h, welding 3 h and finishing 1.5 h. You add 10% for delays. What time should you plan for?
options: 8 hours 48 minutes
8 hours
9 hours 30 minutes
8 hours 10 minutes

questions.stem: Two welders can work on separate parts of a job at the same time. What is the main benefit of planning it this way?
options: Each welder can use the other's PPE
Only one welding machine is then needed
The supervisor no longer needs to check the work
The job finishes sooner, without rushing any of the steps

questions.stem: Painting cannot start until welding and cleaning are done. What does this mean for the schedule?
options: Painting can be done first to save time
Painting and welding can be done together
Any delay to them delays the painting
Painting can be left off the schedule

questions.stem: What is a 'milestone' in a job schedule?
options: The distance from the shop to the site
The heaviest piece in the fabrication
A list of all the tools needed for the job
A key point, such as 'frame welded'

questions.stem: Why should a plan include a back-up for key resources, such as a spare welding machine or a second supplier?
options: So that the team can use two machines at once
So that the client pays for the extra machine
So work can go on if something fails
So that the first supplier will lower the price

questions.stem: Your plan needs the plasma cutter on Tuesday, but another team has booked it. What is the best action?
options: Use it anyway, as your job is more important
Cut everything by hand, whatever the time it takes
Agree a time with them, or change the order of work
Wait until next week, when it is free all day

questions.stem: Galvanised bolts must come from Kingston and take 5 working days. The job starts in 3 days. What should the plan do?
options: Order now, and do the work that needs no bolts first
Start the job and hope the bolts arrive early
Use any bolts found in the scrap bin instead
Put off the whole job until the bolts arrive

questions.stem: Why should the labels or certificates on steel be checked before it is used on a job with a specification?
options: To find out which truck delivered it
To confirm the grade and size
To check how much the supplier charged for it
To decide which end of the bar to cut first

questions.stem: Why should the plan list consumables, such as grinding discs, electrodes, wire and gas?
options: They are free, so the client does not need to know
They are only needed for very large jobs
The supplier will refuse to deliver without a list
They run out fast, and a shortage can stop the job

questions.stem: The welding procedure calls for low-hydrogen electrodes. What must the plan include?
options: Keeping the electrodes in the open so they stay cool
Dry storage, such as a rod oven, as the maker says
Dipping the electrodes in water before use
Buying them only on the day they are needed

questions.stem: The job is to weld a bracket on to a steel tank that once held diesel. What must the plan include before any hot work?
options: Welding quickly, so the tank does not get hot
Having it cleaned, tested and permitted first
Filling the tank with oxygen to clear the fumes
Welding only on the side away from the opening

questions.stem: When the hazards of a job are assessed, why is the job broken into steps first?
options: So that each step can be given to a different team or shift
So the hazards of each step can be found and controlled
So that the job looks bigger to the client
So that the steps can be done in any order

questions.stem: The plan includes welding galvanised parts indoors. Which control should be planned?
options: An open door at the far end of the shop
Fume extraction at the weld
A dust mask of the kind used for sanding
Welding faster so that less fume is made

questions.stem: You will fit a railing at a guest house in Ocho Rios while guests are staying there. What should the plan include?
options: Agreed working times, barriers and screens round the work
Working at night, so that guests do not see the team
Asking guests to move out of their rooms for the day
Leaving all tools on site overnight to save time

questions.stem: A gate must be fitted at a house up a narrow lane in Portland. Why should you visit or ask about the site before the day?
options: To meet the neighbours and tell them the price of the gate
To decide what colour the gate should be
To count how many trees are near the house
To plan the transport, access, power and set-up

questions.stem: There is no mains power at a site in rural St Elizabeth. What must the plan provide?
options: A generator or engine welder, with fuel
A long extension lead from the nearest shop
Battery tools only, for all the welding work
A power cable joined to the overhead lines

questions.stem: Why should the plan name one person in charge on a site job?
options: So that the others can take longer breaks
So that only one person needs to wear PPE
So one person decides and is the contact
So that person can do all of the welding

questions.stem: Which is best when you share out the tasks in your team plan?
options: Give the hardest task to the newest trainee
Let everyone choose, and keep the easy tasks
Give all the tasks to the fastest welder in the team
Match tasks to skills, and support the trainees

questions.stem: How should a team leader brief the team on the plan?
options: Pin the plan on the wall and say nothing about it
Tell only the most senior welder
Read it out quickly at the end of the day, then leave
Go over steps, roles and hazards, then take questions

questions.stem: Why should the planned start and finish dates be confirmed with the client?
options: So the client can prepare the site and plan around it
So that the client can be charged for waiting time
So that the team can start whenever it suits the team
So the client cannot complain about the price

questions.stem: Halfway through the day, the job is two hours behind the plan. What should the team leader do first?
options: Tell the team to skip the quality checks
Find the cause, and agree a new plan
Say nothing and hope to catch up tomorrow
Send half the team home to save on wages

questions.stem: Which check should be made during the fit-up of a rectangular frame, before welding?
options: Weigh the frame to check it is not too heavy
Paint the corners so that rust does not start
Measure the diagonals to check that it is square
Count the electrodes left in the packet for the job

questions.stem: Why should the plan say who inspects the finished welds, and against which standard?
options: So that the inspector can be blamed for any faults
So that the welders do not need to look at their work
So that the inspection can be left out if time is short
So the right checks are done and recorded

questions.stem: Why should a change to the job be agreed in writing before work on it starts?
options: So the cost, time and details are clear to both sides
So that the change can be done without a drawing
So the team can charge any price it chooses
So that the original plan can be thrown away

questions.stem: The job includes painting a gate outdoors in the rainy season. What should the plan allow for?
options: Rain delays, and a dry, covered place to paint
Painting faster, so the rain cannot reach it
Painting over the wet steel, to save waiting time
No change, as paint dries in any weather

questions.stem: A gate has 6 m² of surface to paint, and it needs two coats. One litre covers about 10 m² per coat. How much paint is needed?
options: 1.2 litres
0.6 litres
2.4 litres
6 litres

questions.stem: The plan needs 3 lengths of tube at J$4,500 each and 1 packet of electrodes at J$3,200. What is the material cost before GCT?
Two welders work 6 hours each on a job. The labour rate is J$1,200 per hour for each welder. What is the labour cost?
Which documents should go with the team to a site job?
options: Only the invoice, so the client can pay
The drawing, job card, safety plan and checklist
The shop's price list and the staff holiday timetable
Nothing, as the leader can remember it all

questions.stem: When the team arrives on site, what should be done first?
options: Unload everything as fast as possible
Start welding to make up for the travel time
Set up the generator in the nearest doorway
Check that the site is safe and as planned

questions.stem: Why should the plan say how offcuts and waste will be handled?
options: So the client can sell the scrap afterwards
So that offcuts can be left on site for later
To keep the site safe and save useful offcuts
Waste does not need planning on a small job

questions.stem: The work is finished. What must happen before the job card is signed off?
options: It is inspected and any faults are fixed
The team takes photos for social media
The client pays the whole amount in cash
The tools are packed into the van first

questions.stem: Why should a completion report list anything still to be done, such as a part on back order?
options: So it is followed up and the client is not let down
So that the team can be paid twice for the job
So the client does not need to be told about it
So that the job can be closed and forgotten about quickly

questions.stem: Why should the actual hours for each step be recorded beside the planned hours?
options: So that slow workers can be named
So that future plans and quotes use real figures
So that the time sheets look fuller
So that the planned hours can be changed later

questions.stem: Which planning tool shows the steps as boxes joined by arrows, with decision points such as 'Passed inspection?'
options: A cut list
A materials list
A flowchart
A time sheet

questions.stem: You have three jobs: a broken school gate (a safety risk), a new grill due on Friday, and some shelving with no date. Which should be planned first?
options: The shelving, as it is the quickest job
The grill, as it has a firm date
The broken school gate
Whichever job pays the most

questions.stem: Why do experienced welders still use a pre-start checklist for routine jobs?
options: Checklists are only needed by new trainees
The checklist replaces the need to plan
It is easy to skip a step on a routine job
A checklist makes the job go faster every time

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do we call the list of every piece to be cut for a job, with its size and the number needed?
What do the letters JSA stand for, on a form used to plan the safety of each step of a job?
What is the name of the bar chart that shows each task of a job against time?
A job needs 40 m of tube and 46 m is ordered. What percentage extra was allowed?
A frame is 1,600 mm long and 1,200 mm wide. If it is square, what should each diagonal measure, in mm?
What do we call the time between ordering an item and its delivery?
What do we call the extra time or money added to a plan in case of problems?
What is the name of the document that records a change to the job, agreed with the client?
A job uses 2 welders for 7 hours each. How many labour hours is that?
In the letters WPS on a welding job, what does the 'P' stand for?
What do we call the longest chain of linked tasks, which sets the shortest time the whole job can take?
What is the name of the document that comes with steel from the mill, giving its grade and test results?
A job needs 30 labour hours. A team of 3 people works 5 productive hours each per day. How many days will the job take?
What do we call the space left between two plates before a butt weld, as set out in the welding procedure?
What do we call the width of material lost in a saw cut?

essays.stem: You are given a drawing and a job card to make a steel security grill for a window. Describe how you would plan the job from start to finish.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would read the job card and drawing carefully: the sizes, the material, the weld details, the finish, the quantity and the due date, and check that I have the latest revision. I would ask about anything unclear before starting. Then I would list the steps in order: check and collect the material, mark out and cut, prepare the ends, set out and tack the frame, check that it is square, weld in a planned sequence, clean and grind, inspect, prime and paint, and deliver or fit. I would make a cut list with sizes and numbers, allowing for saw cuts, and a list of the consumables, tools and equipment, and check that they are in stock. I would assess the hazards of each step, such as grinding, arc flash and lifting, and plan the controls and PPE. I would estimate the time for each step, add an allowance for delays, and agree the plan with my supervisor. Finally I would plan the checks: the diagonals at fit-up, the weld sizes, and the final inspection against the drawing.
markingPoints: Reads and checks the job card and drawing, including the revision, and clears up doubts
Lists the steps in a sensible order
Makes a cut list and lists the materials, consumables, tools and equipment, and checks stock
Assesses the hazards of each step and plans the controls and PPE
Estimates the time with an allowance, plans the quality checks, and agrees the plan with the supervisor

essays.stem: Explain how to work out the materials, consumables and equipment needed for a fabrication job. Use a worked example.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start from the drawing and make a cut list of every piece: its section, its length and how many are needed. For example, a frame 1,200 mm by 800 mm in 25 mm square tube, with the short sides fitted between the long ones, needs 2 pieces at 1,200 mm and 2 at 750 mm (800 mm less two tube widths). That is 2,400 + 1,500 = 3,900 mm. I would allow about 3 mm for each saw cut, which gives about 3.91 m, so one 6 m stock length is enough. Then I would list the consumables: electrodes or wire, shielding gas, grinding and cutting discs, primer and paint, worked out from the length of weld and the area to be painted, with a little extra for waste. Next I would list the equipment: saw, welding machine, clamps, squares, grinder, PPE and any lifting gear. I would check what is in stock, order the rest early to allow for lead times, and record it all on the job sheet.
markingPoints: Makes a cut list from the drawing: section, length and number of pieces
Allows for saw cuts and waste, and works out the stock lengths needed
Lists the consumables and works them out from the weld length and paint area
Lists the tools, equipment, PPE and any lifting gear
Checks stock and orders early, with a correct worked example

essays.stem: Explain how to estimate the time for a fabrication job and make a simple schedule for a team. Show your working for an example.
essays.modelAnswer: I would break the job into steps and estimate each one from past jobs or the actual hours recorded before. For example, for a small gate: cutting 2 hours, fit-up and tacking 3 hours, welding 4 hours, grinding and cleaning 2 hours, painting 2 hours and fitting on site 3 hours. That is 2 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 16 hours. I would add about 10% for delays, which is 1.6 hours, so I would plan 17.6 hours, rounded up to 18 hours. Then I would see which steps depend on others: welding cannot start until fit-up is done, and the paint must dry before the gate is fitted. Some work can run side by side, for example one person cutting the infill bars while another tacks the frame. With two people, I would set out the steps on a simple bar chart over two or three days, showing who does each step and when. I would mark key points, such as 'frame welded', check progress against the chart each day, and update it if something changes.
markingPoints: Breaks the job into steps and estimates each from experience or records
Adds the times correctly and includes an allowance for delays
Finds which steps depend on others and which can run side by side
Shows the steps, people and days on a schedule such as a bar chart
Tracks progress against the schedule and updates it

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan the safety of a site welding job at a customer's premises.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the day I would find out about the site: the access, where we can park and set up, the power supply, who will be there, and any rules of the owner. I would break the job into steps and do a job safety analysis, listing the hazards such as arc flash to the public, fire, electric shock from leads or a generator, fumes, manual handling, working at height, grinding sparks and traffic. For each hazard I would plan controls in order: do as much welding as possible in the shop, use screens and barriers to keep people away, clear or cover anything that can burn, keep an extinguisher and fire blanket ready, check leads and use protected supplies, set the generator outside with its fuel stored safely, and use proper access equipment. I would arrange a hot work permit if the client needs one, and a fire watch after welding. I would list the PPE, the first aid kit, the emergency numbers and the nearest hospital. On the day I would brief the team and the client, check the site against the plan, and stop work if conditions change.
markingPoints: Finds out about the site beforehand: access, power, people and rules
Breaks the job into steps and finds the hazards, including those to the public
Plans controls in a sensible order, such as shop pre-fabrication, screens, barriers and fire precautions
Plans the permit, fire watch, PPE, first aid and emergency contacts
Briefs the team and client and checks the site on arrival

essays.stem: Explain why a welding sequence is planned for a frame or a long joint, and describe a sequence that limits distortion.
essays.modelAnswer: Welding heats the metal, which expands and then shrinks as it cools. The shrinkage pulls the parts out of line, so a frame can bend, twist or go out of square. If the welds are made in a planned order, the pulls balance each other and distortion is kept small. For a rectangular frame, I would first tack all the corners, check the diagonals, and clamp the frame flat to the bench. Then I would weld opposite corners in turn, for example top left, then bottom right, then top right, then bottom left, rather than going round in order. I would weld one side of each joint, then turn the frame and weld the other side, and let the joints cool between runs. For a long joint, I would use back-step or skip welding: short runs made in a set order along the joint, so that the heat is spread out. I would check the diagonals during welding and correct any movement early.
markingPoints: Explains that heating and shrinking cause distortion
Explains that a planned sequence balances the shrinkage
Tacks, checks square and clamps before welding
Describes welding opposite corners or both sides in turn, with cooling
Describes back-step or skip welding for long joints, and checks during welding

essays.stem: Describe how you would brief a team of four on a job plan and agree each person's role.
essays.modelAnswer: I would meet the team before work starts, in a quiet place, with the drawing, job card and plan in front of us. I would explain the aim of the job, the due date and the quality needed. Then I would go through the steps in order, and the hazards, controls and PPE for each. I would give each person a clear role that matches their skills, for example: Andre cuts and prepares the pieces, Shanice and I fit and tack, Kemar welds, and Marsha, a trainee, grinds and helps with the checks under supervision. I would say who checks what, and when the hold points are, such as the diagonal check before welding. I would ask each person to repeat their task and to ask questions, and invite ideas to improve the plan. I would write the roles on the job card or a board, and have everyone sign the safety plan. During the job I would check in with each person, and at the end we would review how it went.
markingPoints: Briefs before work in a suitable place, with the drawing and plan
Explains the aim, steps, quality, hazards and controls
Gives each person a clear role that matches their skills, with support for trainees
Explains the checks and hold points and who does them
Checks understanding, invites ideas, records the roles and follows up

essays.stem: Explain how to monitor progress against the plan during a job, and what to do when the job falls behind.
essays.modelAnswer: I would check progress at set times, for example mid-morning, after lunch and at the end of the day, against the schedule and its key points, such as 'all pieces cut' or 'frame welded'. I would record the actual time each step took beside the planned time. I would also check quality at the hold points, because rushing to keep up often causes faults. If the job falls behind, I would first find out why: a late delivery, a broken machine, more work than expected, or a gap in skills. Then I would look at the options: change the order of work, move a person to the slow step, borrow equipment, work overtime if it is allowed, or move the finish date. I would not cut out safety or quality checks. I would tell my supervisor as soon as I know of the delay, with the reason and a new plan, and tell the client if the finish date will change. Afterwards I would note the cause, so that future plans allow for it.
markingPoints: Checks progress at set times against the schedule and key points
Records actual against planned times and checks quality at the hold points
Finds the cause of any delay
Chooses sensible ways to recover, without cutting safety or quality
Tells the supervisor (and the client if needed) promptly, with a new plan, and notes the lesson

essays.stem: Describe the quality checks you would plan at each stage of a welded fabrication, from receiving the material to the final inspection.
essays.modelAnswer: When material arrives, I would check it against the order and the drawing: the grade, size and thickness, the labels or mill certificates, and any damage or heavy rust. After cutting, I would check the lengths and the squareness of the cuts against the cut list, and that the edge preparation, such as the bevel angle and root face, matches the welding procedure. At fit-up, I would check the gaps, alignment and diagonals before any full welding; this is a hold point that the supervisor signs. During welding, I would check that the welder uses the right electrodes and settings and that each run is cleaned. After welding, I would inspect the welds for size, undercut, porosity, cracks and spatter, using a fillet gauge, and check the overall sizes and squareness again, because welding can distort the work. Before painting, I would check that the surface is clean. Finally, I would inspect the finished item against the drawing and the specification, record the results on an inspection sheet, and get it signed off.
markingPoints: Checks incoming material against the order and drawing
Checks cut sizes and edge preparation
Checks fit-up gaps, alignment and diagonals as a signed hold point
Checks welding practice during welding, and inspects the finished welds with gauges
Final inspection against the drawing and specification, recorded and signed

essays.stem: The client changes the design halfway through a job. Explain how you would handle the change and update the plan.
essays.modelAnswer: I would listen carefully and write down exactly what the client wants changed, with a sketch if needed. I would not start the change straight away. First I would check its effect: which parts already made are affected, what extra material and time are needed, whether the change affects strength or safety, and whether the drawing needs to be revised by the drafter or engineer. I would tell my supervisor, who would price the change. The client would then be given the extra cost and the new finish date, and asked to agree in writing, for example by signing a variation order. Once it is agreed, I would get the revised drawing, mark the old one as superseded so that it is not used by mistake, and update the cut list, the material order, the schedule and the safety plan. I would brief the team on the change, and record it in the job file, so that the final invoice and inspection match what was agreed.
markingPoints: Records exactly what the client wants, without starting the change at once
Checks the effect on parts, materials, time, cost, strength and safety
Gets the change priced and agreed in writing, such as a variation order
Gets a revised drawing and withdraws the old one
Updates the plan, briefs the team and records the change

essays.stem: Describe how to close out a completed job: the final checks, the clean-up, the records, the completion report and the review.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would carry out the final inspection against the drawing and the specification, fix any faults, and record the results. Then the work area would be cleaned: offcuts sorted for reuse or scrap, waste disposed of correctly, electrode stubs collected, and tools cleaned, checked and returned, with any damaged equipment reported. On a site job, the client's premises would be left clean and the barriers removed. I would complete the records: the job card signed off, the hours and materials used, and the inspection sheet. I would write a short completion report saying what was done, the checks and results, any problems, and anything still open, such as a part on back order. The client would be shown the work and asked to sign it off. Finally, the team would hold a short review: what went well, what took longer than planned and why, and what to change next time. The actual hours would be recorded so that future plans and quotes are more accurate.
markingPoints: Final inspection against the drawing and specification, with faults fixed
Clean-up: waste, offcuts, tools returned, damage reported, site left clean
Completes the job card, hours, materials and inspection records
Writes a completion report including open items, and gets the client's sign-off
Holds a review and records actual hours to improve future plans

practical1.title: Plan a fabrication job from a drawing and present the plan
practical1.brief: As a group, prepare a full work plan for a fabrication job, as a team leader would before work starts. The assessor gives the group a job card, a dimensioned drawing (for example, a steel security grill 1,200 mm × 900 mm in 25 mm square tube with 12 mm square bar infill, to be primed, painted and fitted at a house in Old Harbour), a stock price list in J$ and a blank planning pack. Each member writes at least one part of the plan and then presents it: (1) the cut list, with sizes, numbers and an allowance for saw cuts, and the number of 6 m stock lengths; (2) the list of materials, consumables, tools and equipment, with costs before GCT; (3) the steps in order, with a welding sequence to limit distortion and the hold points for checks; (4) a job safety analysis for the shop work and the site fitting; (5) a time estimate with an allowance for delays, shown as a bar chart with each person's tasks. The group checks each part against the drawing and against each other's work, then presents the whole plan to the assessor in about 15 minutes and answers questions. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the plan to the group's practical.
materials: Job card and dimensioned drawing (from the assessor)
Blank planning pack: cut list, materials list, JSA, schedule and inspection sheets
Flip chart or whiteboard for the presentation
photos: The group reading the drawing and sharing out the parts of the plan
The finished cut list, with the stock lengths worked out
The list of materials and costs
The order of work, with the welding sequence and hold points marked
The bar-chart schedule with names and times
checklist: Read the drawing correctly and asked about anything unclear
Wrote their part of the plan accurately, with correct calculations
Allowed for saw cuts, waste and delays
Put the steps in a sensible order, with a welding sequence and hold points
Found the main hazards and planned suitable controls
Checked another member's part against the drawing
Presented their part clearly and answered questions
safety: This practical is done in the classroom; no tools or machines are used
If the group visits the workshop to look at stock or equipment, wear safety boots and eye protection as the Centre's rules say
Keep walkways clear when using flip charts and boards
Plan only safe methods: the assessor will question any unsafe step in the plan

practical2.title: Plan, carry out, inspect and report on a routine fabrication task
practical2.brief: As a group, plan a routine fabrication task, carry it out to the plan, inspect it and report on it. The task is to make a rectangular frame 600 mm × 400 mm in 25 mm square tube with one centre rail, to the assessor's drawing, using the Centre's welding process (MMAW or GMAW). Stage 1, plan (about 45 minutes): fill in a job sheet with the cut list, the steps in order, the welding sequence, the hazards and controls, the hold points, and the time for each step and who does it. The assessor checks the plan before work starts. Stage 2, make: cut and prepare the pieces, tack the frame on a flat bench, and measure the diagonals. This is a hold point: the assessor signs it before any full welding. Weld out the frame in the planned sequence, then clean and grind. Every member does at least one making step while the assessor watches, and records the actual time it took. Stage 3, inspect: measure the frame against the drawing (sizes, diagonals and flatness), check the welds with a fillet gauge, and record the results on an inspection sheet. Stage 4, report: write a one-page completion report with the results, the planned and actual times, any problems, and what the group would change next time. Clean up the work area. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and documents to the group's practical.
materials: 25 mm × 25 mm square steel tube (about 3 m), and the assessor's drawing
Welding machine and consumables for the Centre's process (MMAW or GMAW)
Saw or cut-off machine as the Centre allows, files and an angle grinder
Tape measure, steel rule, square, clamps and a flat bench
Job sheet, inspection sheet and completion report form
photos: The completed job sheet, checked by the assessor
The pieces cut and laid out against the cut list
The frame tacked, the diagonals being measured, and the signed hold point
Welding in the planned sequence, with full PPE
The inspection: diagonals, sizes and a fillet gauge on a weld
The completed inspection sheet and completion report
checklist: Helped write a clear plan with a cut list, sequence, hazards, hold points and times
Wore the correct PPE and worked safely throughout
Cut and prepared pieces to size, within the tolerance on the drawing
Tacked and checked the diagonals before welding, and waited for the hold point to be signed
Measured and recorded the inspection results accurately
Recorded actual times and helped write the completion report
Cleaned up the work area and returned the tools
safety: Wear full PPE for welding and grinding: helmet with a suitable shade, safety glasses, gloves, jacket and boots
Weld only in a booth or behind screens, and warn others before striking an arc
Check the grinder and disc before use, and keep the guard on
Remove anything that can burn, keep an extinguisher at hand, and treat all metal as hot
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules for each machine
